```{r setup, include=FALSE}
                      fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5)
```

## Background

The St. Louis branch of the Federal Reserve System maintains an extensive
database of U.S. economic data that is available to the public.
Economists, businesses, and financial institutions rely on the Federal
Reserve Economic Data (FRED) database to guide their organizations'
behaviors.

## Objective

In this activity we use the fredr package to pull FRED data directly
into R, then use tidyverse and ggplot2 to analyze and visualize it. The
goal is to understand how the federal funds rate (FFR), long-term
Treasury yields, inflation, unemployment, and the business cycle relate
to one another and to the primary mortgage market.

## Connecting to FRED in RStudio

The fredr, tidyverse, and lubridate packages are loaded and the FRED API
key is set in chunks hidden from this report (`include = FALSE`), so the
key is not published.

```{r packages, include = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(fredr)
library(ggplot2)
```

```{r api_key, include = FALSE}
fredr_set_key("479b16811497819c8a48b976ed38a94e")
```

### Analysis window

Every plot covers the same rolling 20-year window, ending at the date
the document is knit.

```{r dates}
end_date   <- Sys.Date()
start_date <- floor_date(end_date %m-% years(20), unit = "month")

start_date
end_date
```

### Helper functions

Two user-defined functions keep the code for tasks 1-4 short and
consistent. `get_series()` downloads one FRED series and tags it with a
readable label; `plot_series()` draws a formatted line chart.

```{r helpers}
get_series <- function(series_id, label, ...) {
  fredr( series_id = series_id, observation_start = start_date, observation_end = end_date,
    ...) %>%
    select(date, value) %>%
    filter(!is.na(value)) %>%
    mutate(series = label)
}

plot_series <- function(df, title, y_label, colors) {
  ggplot(df, aes(x = date, y = value, color = series)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
    scale_color_manual(values = colors) + scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 years", date_labels = "%Y") + labs(title = title, x = "Observation Date", y = y_label, color = "Series", caption = "Source: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis") + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),legend.position = "bottom")
}
```

## Search for Data

```{r search}
popular_funds_series <- fredr_series_search_text( search_text = "federal funds", order_by    = "popularity", sort_order = "desc", limit = 5)

string_of_results <- paste(popular_funds_series$id, collapse = ", ")
print(paste("The top series id are:", string_of_results))
```

The series used in this report are:

| Task | Measure                            | FRED Series ID | Frequency                       |
|------|------------------------------------|----------------|---------------------------------|
| 1    | Effective federal funds rate       | FEDFUNDS       | Monthly                         |
| 2    | 10-year Treasury constant maturity | GS10           | Monthly                         |
| 3    | CPI, all items (headline)          | CPIAUCSL       | Monthly, % change from year ago |
| 3    | CPI less food and energy (core)    | CPILFESL       | Monthly, % change from year ago |
| 4    | Civilian unemployment rate         | UNRATE         | Monthly                         |
| 5    | NBER recession indicator           | USREC          | Monthly (1 = recession)         |
| 6    | 30-year fixed mortgage average     | MORTGAGE30US   | Weekly, averaged to monthly     |
## Analysis Tasks

You are a financial analyst at a bank that sells mortgages on the
primary market. Your manager wants to understand how historical data can
serve as an indicator of the federal funds rate (FFR). The FFR is one of
several factors that drive the prime rate for home mortgages. Tasks 1-6
below plot the FFR, the 10-year Treasury rate, inflation, unemployment,
and U.S. recessions over the past 20 years, then combine them into a
single money-plot used to analyze the mortgage market and forecast the
FFR.

## Task 1: Federal Funds Rate, Past 20 Years

```{r task1}
# Save the #1 search result's series ID, as in the template ("FEDFUNDS")
popular_funds_series_id <- popular_funds_series$id[1]

# Template pipe example, with dates updated to the past 20 years
popular_funds_series_id %>%
  fredr( observation_start = start_date, observation_end = end_date) %>%
  ggplot(data = ., mapping = aes(x = date, y = value, color = series_id)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + labs(x = "Observation Date", y = "Rate (%)", color = "Series",
caption = "Source: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis") + ggtitle("Federal Funds Rate\n(Effective)") + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"), legend.position = "bottom")

# Save the same series for the money-plot in Task 6
FFR_data <- get_series(popular_funds_series_id, "Effective Fed Funds Rate")
```

The FFR shows three distinct regimes: a pre-crisis peak above 5% in
2006-07, more than a decade pinned near zero after the 2008 financial
crisis (with a brief, modest hiking cycle in 2016-18), and the
aggressive 2022-23 tightening cycle that took the rate back above 5%
before cuts resumed in late 2024 and 2025.

## Task 2: 10-Year Treasury Rate, Past 20 Years

```{r task2}
T10_data <- get_series("GS10", "10-Year Treasury")

plot_series(T10_data, title = "10-Year Treasury Constant Maturity Rate", y_label = "Yield (%)", colors  = c("10-Year Treasury" = "#2e7d32"))
```

The 10-year yield is set by the bond market rather than the Fed. It
reflects expected future short rates, expected inflation, and a term
premium. It moved far less than the FFR during the zero-rate years and
reached its low in 2020 before rising sharply alongside inflation.

## Task 3: Inflation Rate, Past 20 Years

Inflation is measured as the percent change in the Consumer Price Index
from one year earlier. Core CPI removes volatile food and energy prices
and is a better gauge of underlying trend.

```{r task3}
CPI_data <- bind_rows( get_series("CPIAUCSL", "Headline CPI", units = "pc1"), get_series("CPILFESL", "Core CPI", units = "pc1"))

plot_series(CPI_data, title = "Inflation Rate (CPI, Year-over-Year % Change)", y_label = "Inflation (%)", colors  = c("Headline CPI" = "#c62828", "Core CPI" = "#ef9a9a")) +  geom_hline(yintercept = 2, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") + annotate("text",x = as.Date("2024-01-01"), y = 1.4, label = "Fed 2% target", size = 3, color = "grey30", hjust = 0)
```

Headline inflation briefly turned negative in 2009 as energy prices
collapsed, ran close to the 2% target for most of the 2010s, then surged
to roughly 9% in mid-2022, the highest in four decades. It has since
come down but has not returned to target.

## Task 4: Unemployment Rate, Past 20 Years

```{r task4}
UNRATE_data <- get_series("UNRATE", "Unemployment Rate")

plot_series(UNRATE_data, title = "Civilian Unemployment Rate", y_label = "Unemployment (%)",  colors  = c("Unemployment Rate" = "#6a1b9a"))
```

Unemployment peaked near 10% after the Great Recession and took most of
a decade to recover. The 2020 pandemic spike to about 15% was the
sharpest in the post-war record but also the fastest recovery.

## Task 5: Timeline of U.S. Recessions, Past 20 Years

FRED's `USREC` series equals 1 in months the National Bureau of Economic
Research (NBER) classifies as recessionary. The code below turns that
monthly 0/1 series into start and end dates for each recession.

```{r task5}
USREC_data <- get_series("USREC", "Recession")

# Number each run of 0s and 1s, keep the 1s, and find each recession's dates
recessions <- USREC_data %>%
  mutate(spell = cumsum(value != lag(value, default = 0))) %>%
  filter(value == 1) %>%
  group_by(spell) %>%
  summarise(start = min(date), end = max(date) %m+% months(1))

knitr::kable(
  recessions %>%
    transmute(`Recession start` = format(start, "%b %Y"), `Recession end` = format(end - 1, "%b %Y")), caption = "NBER-dated U.S. recessions in the analysis window")

ggplot(USREC_data, aes(x = date, y = value, fill = series)) + geom_col(width = 31) + scale_fill_manual(values = c("Recession" = "grey40")) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 1), labels = c("Expansion", "Recession")) + scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 years", date_labels = "%Y") + labs(title = "Timeline of U.S. Recessions (NBER)", x = "Observation Date", y = NULL, fill = NULL, caption = "Source: FRED series USREC") + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +   theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"), legend.position = "bottom")
```

The window contains two recessions: the Great Recession (December 2007
peak to June 2009 trough, about 18 months) and the very short COVID-19
recession (February 2020 peak to April 2020 trough). In both cases the
Fed cut the FFR to near zero, and in both cases unemployment rose
sharply.

## Task 6: The Money-Plot

### Additional data: the 30-year mortgage rate

Because the manager's question is about the mortgage market, the
money-plot adds Freddie Mac's 30-year fixed mortgage average. FRED
publishes it weekly, so we ask FRED to average it to monthly to match
the other series.

```{r mortgage}
MORT_data <- get_series("MORTGAGE30US", "30-Year Mortgage", frequency = "m", aggregation_method = "avg")
```

### Building the money-plot

The money-plot is built in labeled steps. Each step adds one layer to
the plot object, and the final line displays the finished chart.

```{r moneyplot, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5.5}
# Combine the five series into one data set for plotting
money_df <- bind_rows( 
  FFR_data    %>% mutate(series = "Fed Funds Rate"),
  T10_data    %>% mutate(series = "10-Year Treasury"),
  MORT_data   %>% mutate(series = "30-Year Mortgage"),
  CPI_data    %>% filter(series == "Headline CPI") %>%
                  mutate(series = "CPI Inflation (YoY)"),
  UNRATE_data %>% mutate(series = "Unemployment Rate")) %>%
  mutate(series = factor(series, levels = c("30-Year Mortgage", "10-Year Treasury", "Fed Funds Rate", "CPI Inflation (YoY)", "Unemployment Rate")))

# Color and line style for each series
money_colors <- c("30-Year Mortgage" = "#e65100", "10-Year Treasury" = "#2e7d32", "Fed Funds Rate" = "#1f4e79", "CPI Inflation (YoY)" = "#c62828", "Unemployment Rate" = "#6a1b9a") 

money_lines <- c("30-Year Mortgage" = "solid", "10-Year Treasury" = "solid", "Fed Funds Rate" = "solid", "CPI Inflation (YoY)" = "dashed", "Unemployment Rate" = "dotted")

# Step A: Pipe the data into ggplot and map the columns
money_plot <- money_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = value, color = series, linetype = series))

# Step B: Shade the recessions in the background
money_plot <- money_plot + geom_rect(data = recessions, inherit.aes = FALSE, aes(xmin = start, xmax = end, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "NBER recession"), alpha = 0.35)

# Step C: Add a zero reference line and the five data lines
money_plot <- money_plot + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey60", linewidth = 0.3) +  geom_line(linewidth = 0.85)

# Step D: Set the colors, line styles, and recession shading color
money_plot <- money_plot + scale_color_manual(values = money_colors) + scale_linetype_manual(values = money_lines) + scale_fill_manual(values = c("NBER recession" = "grey75"))

# Step E: Format the date and percent axes
money_plot <- money_plot + scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 years", date_labels = "%Y") + scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(-2, 16, 2))

# Step F: Add the title, subtitle, axis labels, and source caption
plot_subtitle <- paste("Monthly data,", format(start_date, "%b %Y"), "to", format(max(money_df$date), "%b %Y"))

money_plot <- money_plot + labs(title    = "The Money-Plot: Policy Rates, Market Rates, and the Business Cycle",
       subtitle = plot_subtitle,
       x        = "Observation Date",
       y        = "Percent",
       color    = NULL,
       linetype = NULL,
       fill     = NULL,
       caption  = "Sources: FRED (FEDFUNDS, GS10, MORTGAGE30US, CPIAUCSL, UNRATE, USREC)")

# Step G: Arrange the legend and apply the theme
money_plot <- money_plot + guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 2), linetype = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),  plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5), legend.position = "bottom")

# Step H: Display the finished plot
money_plot
```

### Supporting numbers

```{r money_stats}
# Put each series in its own column, keeping months where all five exist
wide <- money_df %>%
  select(date, series, value) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = series, values_from = value) %>%
  drop_na()

cor_mort_10y  <- cor(wide$`30-Year Mortgage`, wide$`10-Year Treasury`)
cor_mort_ffr  <- cor(wide$`30-Year Mortgage`, wide$`Fed Funds Rate`)
spread        <- wide$`30-Year Mortgage` - wide$`10-Year Treasury`
avg_spread    <- mean(spread)
latest_spread <- last(spread)

knitr::kable(tibble(Measure = c("Correlation: mortgage rate vs. 10-year Treasury",  "Correlation: mortgage rate vs. fed funds rate", "Average mortgage minus 10-year spread (pct. points)",   "Latest mortgage minus 10-year spread (pct. points)"), Value = round(c(cor_mort_10y, cor_mort_ffr, avg_spread, latest_spread), 2)), caption = "How closely mortgage rates track each benchmark")

money_df %>%
  group_by(series) %>%
  slice_max(date, n = 1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  transmute(Series = series, `Latest month` = format(date, "%b %Y"), `Value (%)` = value) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, caption = "Most recent observation for each series")
```

### Why the money-plot is built this way

The plot puts every series on one shared percent axis so that the
reader can compare levels directly: how far the mortgage rate sits above
the 10-year Treasury, whether the policy rate is above or below
inflation, and where unemployment is relative to its history. The
30-year mortgage rate is added because it is the price our bank actually
sells, so the question "what drives it?" should be answerable from the
picture. Recessions are shaded in the background rather than drawn as a
line, so they frame the story without competing with the rates. Market
and policy rates are drawn as solid lines, while the two macro
indicators the Fed reacts to (inflation and unemployment) are dashed
and dotted, which separates "what the Fed watches" from "what borrowers
pay." Unemployment and inflation are kept on the same axis instead of a
second axis, because dual axes make it easy to imply relationships that
are only an artifact of scaling.

### Analysis of the mortgage market

**The Fed sets the short end; the bond market sets mortgage rates.** The
30-year mortgage rate moves almost in lockstep with the 10-year
Treasury (correlation of `r round(cor_mort_10y, 2)`), and much less
tightly with the FFR (`r round(cor_mort_ffr, 2)`). Mortgages are priced
off long-term yields because most 30-year loans are refinanced or paid
off in roughly a decade and are funded through mortgage-backed
securities that compete with Treasuries for investors. Over the window
the mortgage rate averaged about `r round(avg_spread, 2)` percentage
points above the 10-year yield; the latest spread is
`r round(latest_spread, 2)` points.

**The FFR still matters, through expectations.** The FFR influences the
10-year yield through expected future short rates, and the plot shows
this clearly in the 2022-23 cycle: as the Fed raised the FFR from near
zero to above 5%, the 10-year and the mortgage rate roughly doubled to
their highest levels in two decades. The reverse case is just as
instructive. The Fed cut the FFR by 1.75 percentage points between
September 2024 and December 2025, yet mortgage rates barely fell,
because long-term yields stayed high on persistent inflation and
heavy Treasury issuance. Cutting the FFR does not guarantee cheaper
mortgages.

**Recessions are when the FFR falls fastest.** In both shaded periods
the Fed cut aggressively as unemployment rose, and mortgage rates
eventually followed long yields down, which set off refinancing booms
in 2009-12 and 2020-21. Rising unemployment is the most reliable
historical signal that the FFR is about to fall.

**Real rates explain the Fed's stance.** When CPI inflation is above the
FFR (most of 2021-22), policy is loose; when the FFR is above inflation
(2023-24), policy is restrictive. Today the two lines sit close
together, which means policy is only mildly restrictive in real terms,
and the Fed has responded to the recent re-acceleration in inflation by
leaning toward tighter policy rather than looser.

### Where things stand (October 2026)

The latest data paint a stagflation-tinged picture. Headline CPI
inflation rose to 3.7% year-over-year in September 2026, up from 3.4%
the month before and well above the 2% target. At the same time, the
labor market is cooling: payrolls grew by only about 29,000 in
September and unemployment rose to 4.2%. Despite the soft jobs data,
the FOMC raised the target range by 25 basis points to 3.75%-4.00% on
September 16, 2026, its first hike since July 2023, and the
accompanying projections signaled roughly one more increase before
year-end. In the bond market, the 10-year yield climbed above 5%, its
highest level since 2007, and Freddie Mac's 30-year mortgage average
reached 7.40% in mid-October, up from about 6.3% a year earlier.

### Prediction: the FFR and the mortgage market

It is not possible to know the future, but the plotted history supports
a reasoned base case.

*Federal funds rate.* The Fed is fighting rising inflation while the
labor market softens, a conflict between its two mandates. Historically
the Fed has prioritized inflation once it runs well above target (as in
2022-23), so the base case is one more 25 basis point hike by December
2026, taking the target range to 4.00%-4.25%, followed by a hold through
at least the first half of 2027. Rate cuts become likely only if either
inflation clearly turns down or unemployment rises meaningfully further.
The money-plot shows that once unemployment starts climbing quickly, the
Fed has historically reversed course within months, so a rise toward 5%
unemployment is the main risk to this forecast and would pull cuts
forward into 2027.

*Mortgage rates.* Because mortgage rates track the 10-year Treasury, the
near-term outlook depends on long yields, not the Fed's next move. With
inflation re-accelerating and the 10-year above 5%, the best estimate is
that the 30-year rate stays in roughly a 6.75%-7.75% range over the next
six to twelve months. A meaningful decline below 6.5% would most likely
require a growth scare or recession that pushes investors into
Treasuries.

*Implications for the bank.* Expect weak refinance volume, since most
existing borrowers hold rates well below today's market and have no
incentive to refinance (the "lock-in" effect). Purchase volume should
also stay subdued, because high rates on top of high home prices strain
affordability. Adjustable-rate and buydown products are likely to gain
share as borrowers look for lower initial payments. The bank should be
positioned to capture a refinancing wave quickly if a recession pushes
long rates down, as happened after each shaded period on the
money-plot, while managing rate-lock pipeline risk carefully in the
meantime given how volatile the 10-year has been.
